pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8. Understand that the three digits of a three-digit number are amounts of hundreds, tens and ones (362 = 3 hundreds + 6 tens + 2 ones = 300 + 60 + 2), and that a 0 in any column is a placeholder (706 = 7 hundreds, 0 tens, 6 ones).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 3): 'recognise the place value of each digit in a three-digit number (hundreds, tens, ones)'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.1 'the three digits of a three-digit number represent amounts of hundreds, tens, and ones'; 2.NBT.3 read/write to 1000 in various forms.
• Operational details — Extend the two-digit column model to three columns (H|T|O) with base-ten flats/rods/cubes, place-value counters and arrow cards, keeping build + name + expanded form (300+60+2) synchronised. Give heavy attention to internal zeros (706, 350) because that is where three-digit place value breaks down. Partition and recombine flexibly.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7, emerging): builds 362 in H|T|O and states each digit's value. Tier B (age 7-8, secure): partitions any three-digit number into 300+60+2 and handles an internal zero (706). Tier C (age 8, extending): partitions non-canonically (362 = 300 + 62 = 250 + 112) and explains the placeholder role of 0.
bestPractices: Extend the familiar tens|ones bench to three columns H|T|O so the new hundreds place is seen as 'the same idea again'.
Keep concrete build, number name and expanded form (300+60+2) in lockstep for every number.
Foreground internal/ trailing zeros (706, 350, 300) as placeholders — this is the highest-value practice for three-digit numbers.
Use arrow/place-value cards to overlay 300, 60, 2 into 362 and pull apart, exposing the hidden zeros.
Practise non-canonical partitioning (362 = 300 + 62 = 340 + 22) to build flexibility for later mental calculation.
keyRepresentations: Base-ten flats/rods/cubes in an H|T|O place-value chart
Part-whole model partitioning the whole into H, T, O
0-1000 number line and Gattegno chart (hundreds/tens/ones rows)
commonMisconceptions: Concatenation: writing 300 + 60 + 2 as 30062, or reading digits separately.
Mishandling internal zeros — writing 'seven hundred and six' as 76 or 7006.
Assigning the wrong place value (thinking the 3 in 362 means 3, not 300).
Losing the placeholder: dropping the 0 in 706 or 350.
Transposition of the spoken order vs written columns in larger numbers.

learn.summary: Ages 7-8 build three-digit place value by assembling numbers in a hundreds|tens|ones (H|T|O) layout with base-ten materials, keeping the concrete build, the number name, and the expanded form (300+60+2) synchronised. A central focus is the placeholder zero: internal and trailing zeros (706, 350, 300) are where three-digit place value commonly breaks down, so learners build, partition, and explain why 706 is not 76. Includes arrow/place-value cards, a static reference anchor, two-tier checks with zero traps, and a 'detective' dialogue supplement.

activities.title: H|T|O exchange bench: build, name, expand
feedback: If a learner writes 300 + 60 + 2 as 30062, rebuild in columns and show that stacking the written parts loses the place structure; the columns recombine to a single numeral 362.
If 'seven hundred and six' is built or written as 76 or 7006, point to the empty tens column: the place exists but holds nothing, so a 0 marks it — 706.
If a learner says the 3 in 362 'means three', point to its column: 3 hundred-flats, worth 300.

When a live readout is available, an OPTIONAL linked panel can show the numeral, the words and the expanded form updating together as pieces are added or removed, and a 'clear the tens' action can make the placeholder 0 appear as the number drops 362→302.
When ten of a lower unit are gathered, an OPTIONAL exchange/auto-fuse action can bundle them upward into one higher unit to reinforce the column relationship.
activities.rationale: Direct building across three columns extends the familiar two-digit tens|ones model so the hundreds place reads as 'the same idea again', and emptying a column lets the placeholder zero emerge from the learner's own action rather than being asserted. This is a research-informed design proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'recognise the place value of each digit in a three-digit number (hundreds, tens, ones)'.
The three digits of a three-digit number represent amounts of hundreds, tens and ones (2.NBT.1); read/write to 1000 in multiple forms (2.NBT.3).
Internal and trailing zeros are a key difficulty in three-digit place value and warrant explicit placeholder teaching.
learnerActions: Set up three labelled columns: Hundreds | Tens | Ones.
Build 362 by placing 3 hundred-flats, 6 ten-rods and 2 ones-cubes into the matching columns.
Say the number name aloud ('three hundred and sixty-two') and write the expanded form 300 + 60 + 2.
Now empty the tens column (remove all 6 rods) and read the new number: 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 2 ones = 302. State what the 0 in the tens place means.
Work in reverse: 'Build seven hundred and six.' Leave the tens column empty and write 706, 700 + 0 + 6.
Build and contrast 76, 706 and 760 side by side; say how the columns differ.
Partition the same number more than one way, e.g. 362 = 300 + 60 + 2, 362 = 300 + 62, 362 = 340 + 22, 362 = 250 + 112.
activities.intendedInsight: Each column shows how many hundreds, tens or ones a digit counts, so a digit's value depends on its place; a 0 marks an empty place that still must be held, which is why 706 (7 hundreds, 0 tens, 6 ones) is not 76.

activities.title: Arrow/place-value cards: overlay and pull apart
feedback: If a learner expects a card for every column in 706, show that leaving the tens place empty is exactly what the 0 records.
If the overlay is misaligned, align the right-hand edges so ones sit over ones and the hidden zeros line up under the larger cards.
activities.rationale: Overlaying cards exposes the usually-hidden zeros inside round numbers and connects compact and expanded notation; it complements the bench by making the written structure explicit. Research-informed proposal, not a validated activity.
sourceClaims: The three digits of a three-digit number represent amounts of hundreds, tens and ones (2.NBT.1); read/write to 1000 in multiple forms (2.NBT.3).
Internal and trailing zeros are a key difficulty in three-digit place value and warrant explicit placeholder teaching.
learnerActions: Take place-value (arrow) cards 300, 60 and 2 and overlay them so the smaller cards cover the trailing zeros of the larger, forming 362.
Pull the cards apart to recover the expanded form 300 + 60 + 2.
Repeat with a number containing an internal zero: overlay 700 and 6 to form 706, and notice no tens card is used — the tens place stays 0.
Say which zeros were hidden under which cards.
activities.intendedInsight: The expanded form and the compact numeral are two views of the same number; the trailing zeros inside 300 and 60 are hidden when cards overlap, and a missing card leaves a placeholder 0.

activities.title: Static reference anchor (labelled 362 and 706)
feedback: Tapping or pointing to a digit can highlight its blocks and state its value (e.g. the 3 highlights 3 hundred-flats = 300).
If a learner relies only on the anchor, move them to the bench to build arbitrary numbers themselves.
activities.rationale: A fixed, labelled example cannot be manipulated by the learner, but it still teaches digit-to-value links and names the placeholder role, serving as a reference alongside active building. Research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'recognise the place value of each digit in a three-digit number (hundreds, tens, ones)'.
Internal and trailing zeros are a key difficulty in three-digit place value and warrant explicit placeholder teaching.
learnerActions: Study a labelled picture of 362 built from flats, rods and cubes; for each digit, name its value (3 → 300, 6 → 60, 2 → 2).
Use a companion 706 anchor: open the 'why the 0?' note and read that there are no tens, but the place must be held.
Use these as a reference wall while doing the build and partition tasks.
activities.intendedInsight: A clearly labelled fixed example links each digit to its quantity and names the role of the placeholder zero, giving a stable picture to return to.

activities.title: Place-value detective: explain the zero
feedback: If the explanation only restates '706 is bigger', prompt back to the empty tens column and the value each digit holds.
Accept explanations that name an empty place being held, e.g. 'there are no tens, but the tens place must still be shown.'
activities.rationale: Dialogue is a light supplement that elicits reasoning in the learner's own words; a dialogue can prompt and check a learner's spoken explanation of the placeholder but does not itself elicit the physical building, so it is placed to follow the hands-on work rather than replace it. Research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: Internal and trailing zeros are a key difficulty in three-digit place value and warrant explicit placeholder teaching.
learnerActions: A character keeps 'losing the zero' and reads 706 as 76.
Explain to the character what the 0 is doing and why 706 and 76 are different numbers.
Challenge the character with your own trap, e.g. ask how 350 differs from 35.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why a placeholder is needed consolidates the idea and surfaces whether the learner truly treats 0 as marking an empty place.

activities.title: Two-tier checks with zero traps
feedback: If a learner reads 706 as 76 or says the 0 'does nothing', rebuild 706 with 7 hundred-flats, no tens, 6 ones and contrast 76, 706, 760.
If a learner reads digits at face value ('the 7 just means seven'), give each digit its place (7 hundreds = 700) and partition 485 = 400 + 80 + 5 with blocks.
Treat partitioning without a zero as partial understanding until the 706-type placeholder is handled.

Model answer for the 706 diagnostic (for judging the reason, not for showing before the learner responds): 7 hundreds (700), 0 tens, 6 ones; the 0 shows there are no tens and holds the tens place so the 7 stays in the hundreds.
activities.rationale: A checking task assesses the structure after it is built; pairing each answer with a reason discriminates genuine place-value understanding from face-value digit reading, especially via the 706 placeholder. Recognition and matching alone do not elicit independent production, so build/partition tasks are retained. Research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'recognise the place value of each digit in a three-digit number (hundreds, tens, ones)'.
Internal and trailing zeros are a key difficulty in three-digit place value and warrant explicit placeholder teaching.
learnerActions: Answer value-of-digit items: 'What is the 3 in 362 worth?' (300).
Match a built representation to its numeral, including 706 and 350 zero traps.
For each answer, give a reason: why is 706 different from 76 — what is the 0 doing?
Diagnostic: write 706 and explain what each digit is worth, what the 0 is doing, and how you know.
activities.intendedInsight: Once a number is built, learners can be checked on whether they read digits by place, handle the placeholder zero, and partition flexibly; the reason tier reveals whether the structure is understood or digits are read at face value.

constraints: Keep concrete build, number name and expanded form in lockstep for every number so the three views stay connected.
Give heavy, explicit attention to internal and trailing zeros (706, 350, 300) — this is where three-digit place value commonly breaks down.
Recognition and matching items check structure but do not elicit independent construction; include build and partition tasks where the learner produces the number and states digit values.
The static labelled anchor is a reference scaffold: it cannot let a learner build arbitrary numbers or watch the placeholder emerge, so pair it with active building.
Dialogue is a supplement for eliciting a learner's reasoning; it does not itself produce the physical build, so place it to follow hands-on building.

Flat paper/card items such as overlay cards have slight thickness and are physical approximations of the ideal notation; a screen bench with a live readout is one option, not a requirement, and physical materials can carry the activity equally.
Extend the two-digit model deliberately so the hundreds place is seen as the same idea, not a brand-new rule.

Additional source representations — place-value counters (100/10/1) in labelled columns, a 0–1000 number line, a part-whole model, and a Gattegno chart — may support the same place-value structure and can substitute for or supplement the flats/rods/cubes and arrow cards; the alternative non-canonical partition 362 = 340 + 22 is another valid flexibility example.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row labelled 3D interactive as poor fit, asserting a third dimension 'adds load, not insight'. This comparative/necessity claim is not established by the cited sources; it is omitted as a universal law and treated only as a design preference for a planar place-value layout.

The original recommendation framed the build as 'defeating' the 7006/76 error. Softened: building and explaining the placeholder can address this error, but the sources do not establish that any single artefact defeats a misconception.
CCSS-M (2.NBT.1/2.NBT.3) and the NCETM placeholder claim are marked verified:false in the row; the NC Year 3 claim is marked verified:true. Evidence strength is carried over as-is, not upgraded.
CCSS-M cites Grade 2 standards (2.NBT) while the topic is pitched at UK Year 3 / ages 7-8; the standards align on content but differ in grade labelling — noted for reviewer awareness.

Several source keyRepresentations (0–1000 number line, Gattegno chart, part-whole model, place-value counters) and the alternative partition 362 = 340 + 22 were not built into dedicated activities; they are retained as options in constraints for fidelity rather than dropped.
362 = 250 + 112 requires regrouping 112 into the tens/ones; retained from the source as a Tier C flexibility example but may be too demanding for some learners — noted for reviewer judgement.

probeDeeper: Partition 485 into hundreds, tens and ones.
Why is 706 different from 76 — what is the 0 doing?
Which digit is worth the most in 362, and how much is it worth?
assess.correctAnswer: 7 hundreds (700), 0 tens, 6 ones. The 0 shows there are no tens and holds the tens place so the 7 stays in the hundreds.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the placeholder 0 as meaningless and collapses the number: reads 706 as 76
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build 706 with 7 hundred-flats, no tens, 6 ones; the empty tens spot IS the zero. Contrast 76, 706, 760.
errorPatterns.distractor: 706 is the same as 76 — the 0 does nothing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child ignores the 0 or says '706 is the same as 76'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads digits at face value: 'the 7 just means seven'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Give each digit its place ('7 hundreds = 700') and partition 485 = 400 + 80 + 5 with blocks.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the 7 stands for seven rather than 7 hundreds.

responseLevels.gap: Reads digits at face value or drops the placeholder zero (706 → 76).
responseLevels.full: States each digit's value including the placeholder 0, and partitions/recombines any three-digit number by place.
responseLevels.partial: Partitions numbers without a zero but mishandles the placeholder in 706-type numbers.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Write 706. Ask: 'What is each digit worth here — and what is the 0 doing? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The placeholder zero in 706 splits children cleanly: those with three-digit place value explain the 0 marks an empty tens column; those without either drop it (reading 76) or treat digits at face value. The reason tier surfaces which.
